::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- explain why a **linear** projection such as PCA cannot unroll curved structure;
- describe in plain words how **t-SNE** and **UMAP** build a map that keeps **neighbours** together;
- run `Rtsne::Rtsne()` and `uwot::umap()`, and judge how **perplexity**, **`n_neighbors`**, **`min_dist`** and the **seed** change the result;
- say what you **can** and **cannot** read from a t-SNE or UMAP plot, and measure **how many neighbours** a map preserves;
- use UMAP coordinates as model features **without leakage** (`ret_model = TRUE` + `umap_transform()`).
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(Rtsne)   # t-SNE
library(uwot)    # UMAP
```

## 1. Why non-linear embeddings?

PCA and classical MDS draw a map by **projecting** the data onto a flat plane: they look at the cloud of points from the best possible angle. That works when the interesting structure is roughly flat. It fails when the data lie on a **curved surface** folded inside the higher-dimensional space.

The classic example is the **swiss roll**: a flat sheet of paper rolled up like a cake. Two points on neighbouring layers of the roll can be close in a straight line, but far apart if you walk along the paper. A good 2-D map should **unroll** the sheet. Let's build one in base R. Each point has a position `t` along the roll and a height `h`; the roll lives in three dimensions.

```{r}
#| label: swiss-roll
set.seed(1)
n_roll <- 800
t <- runif(n_roll, 1.5 * pi, 4.5 * pi)   # position along the roll
h <- runif(n_roll, 0, 20)                # height of the sheet
roll <- cbind(x = t * cos(t), y = h, z = t * sin(t)) +
  matrix(rnorm(3 * n_roll, sd = 0.2), ncol = 3)   # a little noise

# the "true" flat sheet: distance walked along the paper, and height
arc <- 0.5 * (t * sqrt(1 + t^2) + asinh(t))
sheet <- cbind(arc, h)
```

`arc` is the length of the spiral from its centre to each point, so `sheet` is what we would get by unrolling the paper perfectly. Now PCA:

```{r}
#| label: fig-roll-pca
#| fig-cap: "Left: PCA of the 3-D swiss roll, coloured by position along the roll. Right: the unrolled sheet we would like to recover."
pca_roll <- prcomp(roll)

bind_rows(
  data.frame(pca_roll$x[, 1:2], position = arc, map = "PCA (PC1, PC2)"),
  data.frame(PC1 = arc, PC2 = h, position = arc, map = "True unrolled sheet")
) |>
  ggplot(aes(PC1, PC2, colour = position)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  facet_wrap(~ map, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Dimension 1", y = "Dimension 2", colour = "Position on roll")
```

PCA keeps the two directions with the most variance — here the two axes across the spiral — and drops the height. We see the roll from one end: the colours wind around in a spiral instead of running in one direction, points on neighbouring layers are only a few units apart although they are far apart along the paper, and points at all heights are squashed on top of each other. **No rotation of a flat projection can unroll the sheet**, because the problem is curvature, not orientation.

Non-linear embedding methods take a different approach: instead of preserving *all* distances, they try to preserve **who is whose neighbour**. If two points are close on the paper they should be close on the map; how far apart distant points end up matters much less.

## 2. Measuring "neighbours kept"

Before trying new methods, let's write a yardstick. For every point we find its $k$ nearest neighbours in the original space and its $k$ nearest neighbours on the map, and count how many are shared. The average fraction is the **neighbourhood preservation** (also called *k-NN recall*). It is 1 if the map keeps every neighbourhood, and close to $k/(n-1)$ — almost 0 — for a random map.

```{r}
#| label: knn-preserved
knn_preserved <- function(high, low, k = 10) {
  d_high <- as.matrix(dist(high))
  d_low  <- as.matrix(dist(low))
  diag(d_high) <- Inf                      # a point is not its own neighbour
  diag(d_low)  <- Inf
  shared <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(d_high)), \(i) {
    nn_high <- order(d_high[i, ])[1:k]
    nn_low  <- order(d_low[i, ])[1:k]
    length(intersect(nn_high, nn_low))
  }, numeric(1))
  mean(shared) / k
}

knn_preserved(roll, pca_roll$x[, 1:2])   # PCA map
knn_preserved(roll, sheet)               # perfectly unrolled sheet
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- On the PCA map, on average only `r round(100 * knn_preserved(roll, pca_roll$x[, 1:2]))`% of each point's 10 nearest neighbours are still among its 10 nearest neighbours.
- The unrolled sheet keeps `r round(100 * knn_preserved(roll, sheet))`% (not 100% only because of the noise we added).
- A random 2-D map would keep about `r round(100 * 10 / (n_roll - 1), 1)`%.
:::

`dist()` on $n$ points builds an $n \times n$ table, so this function is fine for a few thousand points; for larger data, compute it on a random subsample.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: trustworthiness and continuity

Our measure counts shared neighbours. Two classical, rank-based refinements are due to Venna and Kaski. Let $r(i, j)$ be the rank of $j$ among the neighbours of $i$ in the original space, and $U_k(i)$ the points that are among the $k$ nearest neighbours of $i$ **on the map but not in the original space** ("intruders"). Then

$$
T(k) = 1 - \frac{2}{nk(2n - 3k - 1)} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j \in U_k(i)} \big(r(i, j) - k\big).
$$

**Trustworthiness** $T(k)$ penalises false neighbours on the map, more heavily the farther away they really are. **Continuity** is the mirror image: it penalises true neighbours that the map pushed away. Both equal 1 for a perfect map. Our simpler `knn_preserved()` treats the two kinds of error together and ignores how bad each mistake is.
:::

## 3. The idea behind t-SNE

**t-SNE** (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbour Embedding) works in three steps.

1. **Neighbour probabilities in the original space.** For each point $i$, imagine it picks a neighbour at random, preferring close points. Close points get a high probability, far points almost zero. How quickly the probability fades with distance is tuned separately for every point.
2. **Neighbour probabilities on the map.** On a 2-D map, the same kind of probabilities are computed from the map distances, but with a **heavy-tailed** curve (the Student t distribution with one degree of freedom).
3. **Move the points.** Starting from a random layout, t-SNE moves the points step by step to make the two sets of probabilities as similar as possible. The mismatch is measured by the **Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence**.

### Perplexity: the effective number of neighbours

The main setting is the **perplexity**. Roughly, it is the **number of neighbours** each point pays attention to. For each point, t-SNE chooses the width $\sigma_i$ of a Gaussian "bump" so that the neighbour probabilities have the requested perplexity. Let's do this ourselves for one penguin.

```{r}
#| label: peng-data
num_vars <- c("bill_len", "bill_dep", "flipper_len", "body_mass")

peng <- penguins |>
  select(species, all_of(num_vars)) |>
  na.omit()

peng_x <- scale(peng[, num_vars])   # standardise, as for PCA
dim(peng_x)
```

```{r}
#| label: perplexity
neighbour_probs <- function(d, sigma) {
  w <- exp(-d^2 / (2 * sigma^2))
  w / sum(w)
}
perplexity_of <- function(p) {
  p <- p[p > 0]
  2^(-sum(p * log2(p)))           # 2 to the power of the entropy
}

perplexity_of(rep(1 / 30, 30))    # equal weight on 30 points

d1 <- as.matrix(dist(peng_x))[1, -1]   # distances from penguin 1
sapply(c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1), \(s) perplexity_of(neighbour_probs(d1, s)))
```

If a point spreads its attention **equally** over 30 neighbours, the perplexity is exactly 30: that is why it is read as an "effective number of neighbours". For penguin 1, a narrow bump ($\sigma = 0.1$) gives a perplexity of about `r round(perplexity_of(neighbour_probs(d1, 0.1)), 1)`, a wide one ($\sigma = 1$) about `r round(perplexity_of(neighbour_probs(d1, 1)))`. t-SNE finds the right $\sigma_i$ by a simple search:

```{r}
#| label: find-sigma
find_sigma <- function(d, target, lower = 1e-3, upper = 10) {
  for (iter in 1:50) {                     # bisection
    mid <- (lower + upper) / 2
    too_wide <- perplexity_of(neighbour_probs(d, mid)) > target
    if (too_wide) upper <- mid else lower <- mid
  }
  mid
}

sigma_30 <- find_sigma(d1, target = 30)
sigma_30
perplexity_of(neighbour_probs(d1, sigma_30))
```

Points in **dense** regions get a small $\sigma_i$, points in **sparse** regions a large one, so that every point has about the same number of effective neighbours. This is one reason why t-SNE tends to make all clusters look similarly spread out, whatever their real density.

Typical perplexities are between 5 and 50. `Rtsne()` requires the perplexity to be at most $(n - 1)/3$, so with small data sets the perplexity must be small too. There is no universal "x% of $n$" rule: try a few values and keep what is stable.

### Why a heavy-tailed curve on the map?

```{r}
#| label: fig-kernels
#| fig-cap: "Similarity as a function of distance: Gaussian curve (used in the original space) and Student t curve (used on the map)."
data.frame(distance = seq(0, 5, by = 0.05)) |>
  mutate(Gaussian = exp(-distance^2 / 2),
         `Student t (1 df)` = 1 / (1 + distance^2)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-distance, names_to = "curve",
                      values_to = "similarity") |>
  ggplot(aes(distance, similarity, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Distance", y = "Similarity (unnormalised)", colour = NULL)
```

In many dimensions there is a lot of room; on a plane there is not. If the map used the same Gaussian curve, moderately distant points would be crowded on top of each other (the *crowding problem*). The t curve decays much more slowly, so moderately distant points can be placed **farther apart** on the map at little cost. The result: tight, well-separated groups.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: the t-SNE objective

In the original space, for point $i$,

$$
p_{j \mid i} = \frac{\exp\!\big(-\lVert x_i - x_j \rVert^2 / 2\sigma_i^2\big)}{\sum_{k \ne i} \exp\!\big(-\lVert x_i - x_k \rVert^2 / 2\sigma_i^2\big)},
\qquad
\text{Perp}(P_i) = 2^{H(P_i)},\quad H(P_i) = -\sum_j p_{j \mid i} \log_2 p_{j \mid i},
$$

with $\sigma_i$ chosen so that $\text{Perp}(P_i)$ equals the requested perplexity. The probabilities are symmetrised: $p_{ij} = (p_{j \mid i} + p_{i \mid j}) / 2n$. On the map, with coordinates $y_i$,

$$
q_{ij} = \frac{\big(1 + \lVert y_i - y_j \rVert^2\big)^{-1}}{\sum_{k \ne l} \big(1 + \lVert y_k - y_l \rVert^2\big)^{-1}} .
$$

The map is found by gradient descent on

$$
\text{KL}(P \,\Vert\, Q) = \sum_{i \ne j} p_{ij} \log \frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}} .
$$

The KL divergence is **asymmetric**. Placing true neighbours (large $p_{ij}$) far apart (small $q_{ij}$) is very costly; placing distant points (tiny $p_{ij}$) at any distance costs almost nothing. That is the mathematical reason why t-SNE keeps neighbourhoods but **does not care about large distances**. `Rtsne()` uses the Barnes–Hut approximation (`theta = 0.5`) to speed up the gradient; `theta = 0` computes it exactly.
:::

## 4. t-SNE in R with `Rtsne`

### Duplicates

`Rtsne()` stops with an error if the data contain **duplicate rows** (identical points have distance 0 and nothing to separate them). Check first:

```{r}
#| label: duplicates
anyDuplicated(peng_x)    # 0 means: no duplicated rows
```

The penguins have none. If your data do (the `iris` measurements, for example, contain one repeated flower), you have two options:

- **remove them** before the analysis, e.g. `df[!duplicated(df[, num_vars]), ]` or `distinct()` on the measurement columns with `.keep_all = TRUE` (see Exercise 3), so that the labels stay attached to the rows you keep; this is usually the cleanest choice;
- if you have already removed them, or you want identical points to stay in the data, set `check_duplicates = FALSE`. The check is also slow on large data, so the package documentation suggests removing duplicates yourself and switching it off.

### A first map

```{r}
#| label: tsne-fit
set.seed(42)
tsne_peng <- Rtsne(peng_x, dims = 2, perplexity = 30)
names(tsne_peng)
head(tsne_peng$Y, 3)
```

`Y` holds the 2-D coordinates (one row per penguin, in the same order as `peng_x`). `itercosts` records the KL divergence during the optimisation. By default `Rtsne()` first runs a PCA (`pca = TRUE`, keeping up to `initial_dims = 50` components); with four variables this only rotates the data and changes no distances. `dims = 3` would give a 3-D map.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tsne-peng
#| fig-cap: "t-SNE map of the 342 penguins (perplexity 30), coloured by species."
data.frame(tsne_peng$Y, species = peng$species) |>
  ggplot(aes(X1, X2, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "t-SNE 1", y = "t-SNE 2", colour = "Species")
```

The species were **not** used to build the map; colouring by them afterwards shows that penguins of the same species tend to be each other's neighbours in the four measurements.

### Sensitivity to perplexity and seed

t-SNE is **stochastic**: it starts from a random layout and the result depends on the seed. It also depends on the perplexity.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tsne-perp
#| fig-cap: "t-SNE maps of the penguins with three perplexities (top) and with the same perplexity but two different seeds (bottom)."
run_tsne <- function(perp, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  Y <- Rtsne(peng_x, perplexity = perp)$Y
  data.frame(Y, species = peng$species,
             setting = paste0("perplexity ", perp, ", seed ", seed))
}

bind_rows(run_tsne(5, 42), run_tsne(30, 42), run_tsne(100, 42),
          run_tsne(30, 1), run_tsne(30, 2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(X1, X2, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ setting, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = "t-SNE 1", y = "t-SNE 2", colour = "Species")
```

Look at what changes and what does not. With a **small** perplexity each point only looks at a handful of neighbours, and the map tends to break into many small fragments. With a **large** perplexity the map looks smoother and more "global". Changing the **seed** rotates, mirrors and rearranges the groups. Features that survive all these changes — here, broadly, which penguins end up together — are the ones worth interpreting.

### What you can and cannot read from a t-SNE plot

::: {.callout-important}
## Reading t-SNE (and UMAP) maps

**You can read:** which points are **neighbours**; whether there are **groups** of points that stay together across perplexities and seeds.

**You cannot read:**

- **cluster sizes** — t-SNE adapts $\sigma_i$ to local density, so a tight group and a diffuse group may look equally spread;
- **distances between clusters** — two groups far apart on the map are not necessarily more different than two groups close together;
- **the axes** — "t-SNE 1" has no meaning, no units and no sign; there are no loadings;
- **a few points in a corner as outliers, or apparent clusters in small samples** — t-SNE can create clumps even from random noise, especially with low perplexity.
:::

Also note that `Rtsne()` has **no way to place new points** on an existing map: running it again on more data gives a different map. t-SNE is a tool for **looking**, not for building features.

## 5. UMAP

**UMAP** (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) has the same goal — keep neighbours together — with a different recipe:

1. **Build a k-nearest-neighbour graph.** Each point is connected to its `n_neighbors` nearest points, with weights that fade with distance (adapted to the local density, as in t-SNE).
2. **Lay out the graph in 2-D.** Starting from an initial layout, points are moved so that connected points attract and unconnected points repel. The setting **`min_dist`** says how tightly points may be packed together on the map.

The two settings play roles similar to perplexity:

- **`n_neighbors`** (default 15): small values focus on very local structure (more, smaller groups); large values give a more global, smoother picture;
- **`min_dist`** (default 0.01 in `uwot`): small values pack groups tightly; large values spread points out more evenly.

```{r}
#| label: umap-fit
set.seed(42)
umap_peng <- umap(peng_x, n_neighbors = 15, min_dist = 0.1,
                  n_sgd_threads = 1)
dim(umap_peng)
```

`umap()` returns a matrix with one row per penguin and two columns.

::: {.callout-warning}
## UMAP is stochastic too

UMAP is **not** deterministic: the layout is optimised with random sampling, so different seeds give different maps (an older version of this course said otherwise). For **exactly** reproducible results with `uwot` you need both `set.seed()` and `n_sgd_threads = 1`: with several threads the optimisation runs in an unpredictable order and results differ slightly between runs even with the same seed.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-umap-grid
#| fig-cap: "UMAP maps of the penguins for two values of n_neighbors (rows) and two values of min_dist (columns)."
run_umap <- function(nn, md) {
  set.seed(42)
  Y <- umap(peng_x, n_neighbors = nn, min_dist = md, n_sgd_threads = 1)
  data.frame(Y, species = peng$species,
             n_neighbors = paste("n_neighbors =", nn),
             min_dist = paste("min_dist =", md))
}

bind_rows(run_umap(5, 0.01), run_umap(5, 0.5),
          run_umap(50, 0.01), run_umap(50, 0.5)) |>
  ggplot(aes(X1, X2, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_grid(n_neighbors ~ min_dist, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "UMAP 1", y = "UMAP 2", colour = "Species")
```

Everything said about reading t-SNE plots also applies to UMAP. UMAP layouts often keep the **arrangement** of groups somewhat better than t-SNE, but **neither method reliably preserves global distances**: the distance between two groups on a UMAP map, or the size of a group, should not be interpreted (an older version of this course claimed the opposite). Other useful options are `n_components = 3` for a 3-D map and `metric = "cosine"` for data such as word counts, where the direction of a vector matters more than its length.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: the UMAP objective

For each point $i$ with nearest neighbours $j$, let $\rho_i$ be the distance to its closest neighbour. UMAP sets

$$
w_{j \mid i} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{\max(0, d_{ij} - \rho_i)}{\sigma_i}\right),
\qquad \sum_{j} w_{j \mid i} = \log_2(\texttt{n\_neighbors}),
$$

so every point is connected at least to its nearest neighbour with weight 1, and $\sigma_i$ plays the role of the per-point width in t-SNE. The graph is symmetrised with $v_{ij} = w_{j \mid i} + w_{i \mid j} - w_{j \mid i} w_{i \mid j}$. On the map, similarities are $u_{ij} = \big(1 + a \lVert y_i - y_j \rVert^{2b}\big)^{-1}$, where $a$ and $b$ are derived from `min_dist`. The layout minimises the cross-entropy

$$
\sum_{i \ne j} \left[ v_{ij} \log\frac{v_{ij}}{u_{ij}} + (1 - v_{ij}) \log\frac{1 - v_{ij}}{1 - u_{ij}} \right]
$$

by stochastic gradient descent with **negative sampling** (random pairs are pushed apart) — the source of UMAP's randomness. The second term makes UMAP care a little about non-neighbours, unlike t-SNE, but only through random pairs, so large distances are still not reproduced faithfully.
:::

## 6. PCA vs t-SNE vs UMAP

Let's compare the three maps on both data sets with two numbers: the **neighbourhood preservation** (local structure) and the **rank correlation between all pairwise distances** before and after (global structure; 1 = the map keeps the order of all distances).

```{r}
#| label: compare-fun
dist_cor <- function(high, low) {
  cor(as.vector(dist(high)), as.vector(dist(low)), method = "spearman")
}

embed_scores <- function(high, maps, k = 10) {
  data.frame(
    method      = names(maps),
    knn_kept    = sapply(maps, \(m) knn_preserved(high, m, k = k)),
    dist_rank_r = sapply(maps, \(m) dist_cor(high, m))
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: compare-peng
pca_peng <- prcomp(peng_x)$x[, 1:2]

scores_peng <- embed_scores(peng_x, list(PCA = pca_peng,
                                         `t-SNE` = tsne_peng$Y,
                                         UMAP = umap_peng))
scores_peng
```

```{r}
#| label: compare-roll
set.seed(42)
tsne_roll <- Rtsne(roll, perplexity = 30)$Y
set.seed(42)
umap_roll <- umap(roll, n_neighbors = 15, min_dist = 0.1, n_sgd_threads = 1)

scores_roll <- embed_scores(roll, list(PCA = pca_roll$x[, 1:2],
                                       `t-SNE` = tsne_roll,
                                       UMAP = umap_roll))
scores_roll
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-roll-compare
#| fig-cap: "The swiss roll mapped by PCA, t-SNE and UMAP, coloured by the true position along the roll."
bind_rows(
  data.frame(X1 = pca_roll$x[, 1], X2 = pca_roll$x[, 2], method = "PCA"),
  data.frame(tsne_roll, method = "t-SNE"),
  data.frame(umap_roll, method = "UMAP")
) |>
  mutate(position = rep(arc, 3)) |>
  ggplot(aes(X1, X2, colour = position)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  facet_wrap(~ method, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Dimension 1", y = "Dimension 2", colour = "Position on roll")
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read the comparison

- On the swiss roll, PCA keeps `r round(100 * scores_roll$knn_kept[1])`% of the 10 nearest neighbours, t-SNE `r round(100 * scores_roll$knn_kept[2])`% and UMAP `r round(100 * scores_roll$knn_kept[3])`%. In the figure, check whether the colour runs **smoothly** across each map (sheet unrolled) or jumps (layers mixed). Non-linear methods sometimes **tear** the sheet into pieces: neighbourhoods are kept, but the pieces may be placed in an arbitrary order.
- On the penguins the structure is much less curved. PCA keeps `r round(100 * scores_peng$knn_kept[1])`% of the neighbours, t-SNE `r round(100 * scores_peng$knn_kept[2])`% and UMAP `r round(100 * scores_peng$knn_kept[3])`%.
- The `dist_rank_r` column measures the global picture, using **straight-line** distances. On the swiss roll even the perfectly unrolled sheet scores only `r round(dist_cor(roll, sheet), 2)`, because it keeps distances along the paper, not through the air: always ask *which* distances you want a map to keep. For the penguins, PCA reaches `r round(scores_peng$dist_rank_r[1], 2)`: with four standardised variables, two components already reproduce the order of most distances. The non-linear maps are optimised for neighbours, not for this.
:::

The practical lesson: **start with PCA**. It is fast, deterministic, has interpretable loadings and keeps global distances as well as any 2-D projection can. Reach for t-SNE or UMAP when you mainly care about **local** structure, and judge every map with numbers such as these, not only by eye.

| | PCA | t-SNE | UMAP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linear? | yes | no | no |
| Random result? | no (only signs arbitrary) | yes | yes |
| Main settings | number of components | perplexity | `n_neighbors`, `min_dist` |
| Keeps local neighbours | moderately | well | well |
| Keeps global distances | as well as a projection can | no | not reliably |
| Interpretable axes | yes (loadings) | no | no |
| Can place new points | yes, `predict()` | no | yes, `umap_transform()` |
| Speed on large data | fast | slow | fast |

## 7. UMAP as features, without leakage

Like PCA in [the PCA lesson](50-pca.qmd), UMAP can be a **preprocessing step** for a model: replace the four measurements by two UMAP coordinates and fit a classifier on them. The same rule applies: **everything is estimated on the training data only**. Running UMAP on all penguins and then splitting (as an earlier version of this course did) lets the test penguins shape the map that the model is trained on — the test accuracy becomes optimistic.

`uwot` makes the correct approach easy: `ret_model = TRUE` keeps what is needed to place new points, and `umap_transform()` adds the test points to the **existing** training map without changing it.

```{r}
#| label: umap-split
set.seed(2024)
peng_split <- rsample::initial_split(peng, prop = 0.75, strata = species)
peng_train <- rsample::training(peng_split)
peng_test  <- rsample::testing(peng_split)

# standardise with the TRAINING means and SDs
train_x <- scale(peng_train[, num_vars])
test_x  <- scale(peng_test[, num_vars],
                 center = attr(train_x, "scaled:center"),
                 scale  = attr(train_x, "scaled:scale"))
```

```{r}
#| label: umap-transform
set.seed(2024)
umap_fit <- umap(train_x, n_neighbors = 15, min_dist = 0.1,
                 ret_model = TRUE, n_sgd_threads = 1)
emb_train <- umap_fit$embedding               # training coordinates

set.seed(2024)
emb_test <- umap_transform(test_x, umap_fit, n_sgd_threads = 1)
dim(emb_test)
```

With `ret_model = TRUE`, `umap()` returns a list; the coordinates are in `$embedding`. Now a 5-nearest-neighbour classifier on the UMAP features, and the same classifier on the four standardised measurements for comparison:

```{r}
#| label: umap-knn
pred_umap <- class::knn(train = emb_train, test = emb_test,
                        cl = peng_train$species, k = 5)
pred_raw  <- class::knn(train = train_x, test = test_x,
                        cl = peng_train$species, k = 5)

c(umap_features = mean(pred_umap == peng_test$species),
  raw_features  = mean(pred_raw  == peng_test$species))
```

On the test set the classifier using UMAP features has an accuracy of `r round(mean(pred_umap == peng_test$species), 3)`, compared with `r round(mean(pred_raw == peng_test$species), 3)` on the original variables. With only four informative variables there is little to gain from UMAP; it can help more with many noisy variables. Whether it helps must be checked on held-out data, ideally with cross-validation, and the UMAP settings tuned like any other hyperparameter.

In a tidymodels workflow the `embed` package provides `step_umap()`, which does the same thing inside a recipe (fitted on the training data of each resample):

```{r}
#| label: step-umap
#| eval: false
umap_rec <- recipes::recipe(species ~ ., data = peng_train) |>
  recipes::step_normalize(recipes::all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  embed::step_umap(recipes::all_numeric_predictors(),
                   num_comp = 2, neighbors = 15, min_dist = 0.1)
```

(This chunk is not run here because it needs the `embed` package.) A model with `ret_model = TRUE` contains an index stored outside R; to save it to disk use `uwot::save_uwot()` and `uwot::load_uwot()`, not `saveRDS()`.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Reading cluster sizes and between-cluster distances** from t-SNE or UMAP maps. Only neighbourhoods are (approximately) preserved.
2. **Trusting a single run.** Both methods are stochastic and sensitive to their settings: try several seeds and settings, and interpret only what is stable. For exact reproducibility in `uwot`, use `set.seed()` **and** `n_sgd_threads = 1`.
3. **Forgetting to standardise** variables with different units — exactly as in PCA, the largest numbers dominate the distances.
4. **Duplicated rows** in `Rtsne()`: remove them with `distinct()`, or set `check_duplicates = FALSE` if you know what you are doing. And keep the perplexity at most `(n - 1) / 3`.
5. **Fitting UMAP on all the data before splitting.** Fit on the training set with `ret_model = TRUE` and project the test set with `umap_transform()`. Never use t-SNE coordinates as model features.
6. **Treating clusters on the map as proof of clusters in the data.** Confirm with [clustering methods](../12-clustering/55-clustering-intro.qmd) on the original variables, and with subject knowledge.
:::

## 8. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. On a t-SNE map, group A is twice as wide as group B and far away from group C. What can you conclude?

Very little about size and distance: t-SNE adapts to local density, so widths are not comparable, and distances between groups are not preserved. You *can* conclude that the points within each group tend to be neighbours of each other in the original space — provided the groups are stable across seeds and perplexities.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. What does a perplexity of 30 mean, in plain words?

Each point spreads its neighbour probabilities as if it had about **30 equally likely neighbours**. The width of the Gaussian bump around each point is tuned until this is true.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. A colleague says "UMAP, unlike t-SNE, is deterministic and preserves distances, so it is safe for modelling". Correct both claims.

UMAP is **stochastic** (the layout is optimised with random negative sampling); it is exactly reproducible in `uwot` only with `set.seed()` and `n_sgd_threads = 1`. It preserves **neighbourhoods**, not global distances. It *can* be used to create model features, but only if fitted on the training data and applied to new data with `umap_transform()`, and only if held-out performance shows it helps.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q4. Why can't you use `Rtsne()` coordinates as features in a predictive model?

Because `Rtsne()` cannot place new observations on an existing map. Re-running it with the test data included gives a completely different map (and leaks the test data into the features).
:::

## 9. Exercises

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — predict.** You run `Rtsne()` twice on the same data with the same perplexity, once after `set.seed(1)` and once after `set.seed(2)`. The two maps look like mirror images of each other, and in the second one two groups have swapped places. (a) Is one of the runs wrong? (b) What would make you worried?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) No. The starting layout is random, and t-SNE axes have no meaning: mirror images and rearranged groups are equally good solutions. (b) It would be worrying if the **membership** of the groups changed a lot — e.g. a group present in one run splitting into pieces or merging with another in the other run. That would mean the grouping is not a stable feature of the data.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — perplexity by hand.** Using `neighbour_probs()`, `perplexity_of()` and `find_sigma()` from section 3, find the width $\sigma$ that gives perplexity 5, 30 and 50 for penguin 1. How does $\sigma$ change, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
sapply(c(5, 30, 50), \(p) find_sigma(d1, target = p))
```
The widths are about 0.14, 0.33 and 0.40. A larger perplexity means more effective neighbours, so the Gaussian bump must be **wider** to give non-negligible probability to more points. Repeat for other penguins and you will see that the width needed for the same perplexity differs from point to point, depending on how crowded its region is.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — debug.** This code stops with errors. Find the two problems and fix them.

```r
virginica_x <- scale(iris[101:150, 1:4])
tsne_virginica <- Rtsne(virginica_x, perplexity = 30)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
First, flower 143 has exactly the same four measurements as flower 102, so the data contain a **duplicated row** (`anyDuplicated(virginica_x)` is not 0) and `Rtsne()` refuses to run. Second, with 50 rows the perplexity is too large: it must be at most $(50 - 1)/3 \approx 16.3$. Remove the duplicate and lower the perplexity (and set a seed):
```r
virginica <- iris[101:150, ] |>
  distinct(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, Petal.Length, Petal.Width,
           .keep_all = TRUE)                       # 49 flowers
virginica_x <- scale(virginica[, 1:4])

set.seed(1)
tsne_virginica <- Rtsne(virginica_x, perplexity = 10)  # 10 <= 48 / 3
```
Use the columns of `virginica` (not of `iris`) for labels or colours, so that labels and rows stay aligned.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — how local is "local"?** Compute `knn_preserved()` for the penguin PCA, t-SNE and UMAP maps with `k = 5`, `10` and `50`. How does the ranking of the methods change with `k`? What do you conclude?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
ks <- c(5, 10, 50)
kept <- sapply(ks, \(k) c(
  PCA  = knn_preserved(peng_x, pca_peng, k),
  tSNE = knn_preserved(peng_x, tsne_peng$Y, k),
  UMAP = knn_preserved(peng_x, umap_peng, k)
))
colnames(kept) <- paste0("k = ", ks)
round(kept, 2)
```
For PCA the values are about 0.35, 0.45 and 0.74: the larger the neighbourhood, the easier it is to preserve. t-SNE and UMAP are designed for small neighbourhoods (of the order of the perplexity or `n_neighbors`), so compare their advantage over PCA at `k = 5` with that at `k = 50`: any advantage is expected to be largest for small `k`. The answer to "which map is best?" depends on the scale of structure you care about.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — interpret a silhouette.** A report compares the average **silhouette width** (from `cluster::silhouette()`, a measure of how well-separated known groups are; see the [clustering lessons](../12-clustering/55-clustering-intro.qmd)) of the three species on a PCA map and a t-SNE map of `iris`, and finds a higher value for t-SNE. It concludes that "t-SNE represents the data better". Run the comparison yourself and explain why this conclusion does not follow.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
iris_u <- iris |>
  distinct(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, Petal.Length, Petal.Width,
           .keep_all = TRUE)
iris_x <- scale(iris_u[, 1:4])
set.seed(1)
tsne_iris <- Rtsne(iris_x, perplexity = 30)$Y
pca_iris  <- prcomp(iris_x)$x[, 1:2]

sil <- function(map) {
  mean(cluster::silhouette(as.integer(iris_u$Species), dist(map))[, 3])
}
c(PCA = sil(pca_iris), tSNE = sil(tsne_iris))
```
t-SNE (and UMAP) are designed to produce **tight, well-separated groups**: the heavy-tailed curve pushes moderately distant points apart. A higher silhouette on the map partly reflects this exaggeration, not a better representation of the data. Silhouettes computed on the map also depend on the seed and the perplexity. Better questions are "how many neighbours are kept?" (`knn_preserved()`) and "is the grouping stable across settings?".
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 6 — leakage, measured.** Using the penguin split of section 7, compare the test accuracy of the 5-NN classifier on UMAP features obtained in two ways: (a) the **wrong** way — UMAP on all 342 penguins, then split the coordinates; (b) the **right** way — `ret_model = TRUE` on the training set and `umap_transform()` on the test set. Repeat for 20 different splits. Is the difference large? Why is (a) wrong even when the difference is small?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
one_split <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  idx <- sample(nrow(peng), round(0.75 * nrow(peng)))
  tr  <- scale(peng[idx, num_vars])
  te  <- scale(peng[-idx, num_vars], center = attr(tr, "scaled:center"),
               scale = attr(tr, "scaled:scale"))
  y_tr <- peng$species[idx]
  y_te <- peng$species[-idx]

  all_map <- umap(peng_x, min_dist = 0.1, n_sgd_threads = 1)   # (a) wrong
  pred_a  <- class::knn(all_map[idx, ], all_map[-idx, ], y_tr, k = 5)

  fit    <- umap(tr, min_dist = 0.1, ret_model = TRUE,          # (b) right
                 n_sgd_threads = 1)
  emb_te <- umap_transform(te, fit, n_sgd_threads = 1)
  pred_b <- class::knn(fit$embedding, emb_te, y_tr, k = 5)

  c(wrong = mean(pred_a == y_te), right = mean(pred_b == y_te))
}
res <- sapply(1:20, one_split)
rowMeans(res)
```
On the penguins, whose species are easy to separate, the two averages are likely to be close. Approach (a) is still wrong: the test penguins helped build the map, so their coordinates already "know" where their neighbours in the training set are. The accuracy estimate is then not an honest estimate of performance on truly new penguins, and with harder problems or more variables the optimism can be large.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Idea / function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `knn_preserved(high, low, k)` | fraction of $k$ nearest neighbours kept by a map (our own function) |
| perplexity | t-SNE's effective number of neighbours ($2^{\text{entropy}}$) |
| `Rtsne(x, perplexity = 30)` | t-SNE map in `$Y`; needs no duplicates and perplexity ≤ (n − 1)/3 |
| `umap(x, n_neighbors, min_dist)` | UMAP map (matrix) |
| `set.seed()` + `n_sgd_threads = 1` | exact reproducibility in `uwot` |
| `umap(..., ret_model = TRUE)` + `umap_transform()` | fit on training data, place new points without leakage |
| `embed::step_umap()` | UMAP inside a tidymodels recipe |

- Linear methods cannot **unroll curved structure**; t-SNE and UMAP aim to keep **neighbours** together instead of all distances.
- Both methods are **stochastic** and sensitive to their settings: interpret only what is stable across seeds and settings.
- Neither preserves **cluster sizes** or **distances between clusters** reliably; the axes have no meaning.
- Judge a map with numbers (neighbours kept, distance correlation), and start with **PCA** as a baseline.
- To use UMAP as features, **fit on the training data** and project new data with `umap_transform()`; never use t-SNE coordinates as features.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}

- `uwot` documentation, including the notes on reproducibility, <https://jlmelville.github.io/uwot/>
- McInnes, Healy & Melville, UMAP documentation, "How UMAP works", <https://umap-learn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/how_umap_works.html>
- `Rtsne` reference manual, <https://cran.r-project.org/package=Rtsne>
:::
